newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary needs wage restraint to slash CPI - c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Hungary needs wage restraint to slash CPI - c.bank.

text.p: Hungary needs a wide-ranging consensus by all sections of society on wage restraint to slash year-on-year inflation to about 10 percent in 1998, National Bank of Hungary (NBH) Chairman Gyorgy Suranyi said on Friday.
"For (such a cut) certainly very wide cooperation is necessary and a framework of agreements between interest groups," he told the parliament's economic committee.
He did not detail what this agreement should cover.

Suranyi stressed that the pace of the average rise in nominal wages is one of the most important factors influencing inflation in Hungary, a statement which contrasts sharply with Prime Minister Gyula Horn's comments on Monday which played down the significance of wage hikes in generating inflation.
"It's not wages which increase in inflation but inflation expectations," Horn told reporters.
Suranyi said that last year's price-wage agreements, linking 1997 wage rises to the forecast average inflation of some 17 percent, limited efforts to curb price rises.
He added that Hungary was likely to reduce year-on-year inflation to about 17 percent by December 1997 from 19.8 percent in December 1996.
The government plans to reduce average annual inflation to 17 to 19 percent in 1997 from 23.6 percent last year.

The Finance Ministry, urged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to sharply reduce inflation, said recently the 1998 budget draft may include a larger inflation cut for next year than the originally planned five percentage points.

Analysts and a finance ministry official said recently that the government will have to reach wide-ranging social concensus on a sharp decrease in the pace of wage and price rises in 1998 if it wants to reach a drastic cut in inflation next year.

Horn said earlier this week that the government should follow consistent, predictable economic policies, cooling down high inflation expectations so as to push average inflation down to between nine and 13 percent in 1997.

Suranyi told the committee that Hungary's two-year-old austerity programme stabilised the economy, cut the budget and current account deficits and the foreign state debt, thus enabling the NBH to concentrate on the fight against inflation.
But analysts said the Socialist-Liberal government was in a difficult position if it wanted to curb wage rises ahead of the 1998 general elections,
They added that the prospects of the elections were likely to be heavily felt during wage negotiations and increasing wage pressure would make a drastic inflation cut in 1998 difficult.
